question: According to the World Health Organization, what is the standard age range for adolescence?
explanation: The World Health Organization defines adolescence as the period between 10 and 19 years of age. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T4#GNS312_U3_T4_h1)

question: What marks the biological beginning of the adolescent period?
explanation: Puberty triggers the physical and hormonal changes that officially mark the entry into adolescence. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T4#GNS312_U3_T4_h1)

question: Which hormones primarily drive the physical changes of puberty?
explanation: Sex hormones like estrogen and testosterone are the main chemical drivers of pubertal development. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T4#GNS312_U3_T4_h2)

question: Why do early adolescents often look a bit uncoordinated or clumsy?

options.A: Neurological damage occurs temporarily during puberty
options.B: Hands and feet grow faster than the rest of the body
options.C: Shrinking of the inner ear balancing structures
options.D: Lack of proper physical exercise in school

explanation: Think of it like a growth spurt where the hands and feet shoot up first! This temporary mismatch throws off coordination for a bit, but it completely evens out. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T4#GNS312_U3_T4_h2)

question: Which part of the teenage brain develops much slower than the emotional center?
explanation: The prefrontal cortex (the brain's planning and logic center) takes its time maturing, which explains why teens sometimes act on strong emotions before thinking things through! [learn more](GNS312_U3_T4#GNS312_U3_T4_h3)

question: Why do teenagers often take big risks even when they know it's dangerous?

options.A: They experience a permanent loss of short-term memory
options.B: They completely lack the ability to think logically
options.C: Their cognitive development stops entirely during puberty
options.D: Reward-seeking brain centers develop faster than impulse-control centers

explanation: The thrill-seeking part of the brain develops faster than the brake pedal (impulse control), making exciting experiences feel totally worth the risk to them. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T4#GNS312_U3_T4_h3)

question: What is considered a primary developmental task during adolescence?
explanation: Figuring out who they are outside of the family unit is a central milestone for teenagers. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T4#GNS312_U3_T4_h4)

question: How do teenagers normally show they are trying to be more independent from their parents?

options.A: Refusing to make any decisions on their own
options.B: Questioning family rules and testing personal boundaries
options.C: Completely cutting off all communication with adults
options.D: Seeking total approval for every daily action

explanation: Testing boundaries and questioning authority is a totally normal way teenagers practice thinking for themselves and building autonomy. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T4#GNS312_U3_T4_h4)

question: Which group becomes the main guide for values, styles, and social behavior during the teenage years?
explanation: Friends and peer groups heavily influence how teenagers dress, talk, and act as they search for where they fit in. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T4#GNS312_U3_T4_h5)

question: A 14-year-old patient starts dressing and speaking just like a new group of friends. How should you as a nurse view this?

options.A: An indication of developmental delay in cognitive reasoning
options.B: Evidence of negative peer pressure that requires institutionalization
options.C: A sign of severe psychological personality splitting
options.D: A normal part of peer bonding and identity exploration

explanation: Fitting in with friends is a healthy part of growing up. They are just trying out different styles to see what feels right! [learn more](GNS312_U3_T4#GNS312_U3_T4_h5)

question: Why do adolescent girls need more iron in their diet?

options.A: To balance elevated thyroid hormone levels
options.B: To compensate for menstrual blood loss
options.C: To support rapid brain tissue growth

explanation: Monthly periods mean losing some iron regularly, so young women need iron-rich foods to stay strong and avoid anemia. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T4#GNS312_U3_T4_h6)

question: Which of these is a very common nutrition challenge during the teenage years?

options.A: Development of eating disorders and poor dietary choices
options.B: Complete lack of appetite caused by hormonal stabilization
options.C: Permanent intolerance to all dairy calcium sources
options.D: Inability to absorb basic proteins from food

explanation: Between body image worries and busy school schedules, teens are extra vulnerable to skipping meals, picking junk food, or struggling with eating habits. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T4#GNS312_U3_T4_h6)

question: What makes teenagers feel comfortable enough to seek out reproductive health services?

options.A: Public waiting rooms with adult family members present
options.B: Requiring parental permission for every simple checkup
options.C: Mandatory reporting of all visits to school authorities
options.D: Assured confidentiality and a non-judgmental environment

explanation: Teens want to know their secrets are safe. When they trust their privacy is respected, they are much more likely to seek proper healthcare. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T4#GNS312_U3_T4_h7)

question: As a nurse working in adolescent health, which of these actions should you definitely NOT do?

options.A: Sharing a teenager's private health details with their neighbors
options.B: Screening for risky behaviors in a supportive, private setting
options.C: Providing confidential counseling on sexually transmitted infections
options.D: Educating on the correct use of modern contraceptive methods

explanation: Patient confidentiality is sacred! Gossiping or sharing private health info breaks professional ethics and destroys patient trust immediately. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T4#GNS312_U3_T4_h7)
